analogy.p: The tundra ecosystem is like a person wearing everything they own to survive a blizzard: every layer (climate, soil, plant, animal) has to work with the others, and there is no spare capacity. If you remove one layer, such as the permafrost that holds the water or the lichen that feeds the caribou, the others cannot make up for it. The analogy shows interdependence and fragility. It breaks down because a coat can be put back on, whereas damaged tundra can take decades to regrow.
analogy.t: A tightly packed winter coat with no spare pockets

bullets: **Antarctica** is a continent around the South Pole almost completely covered by a thick ice sheet; it is the coldest, windiest and driest continent.
The **Arctic** is mostly ocean (the Arctic Ocean) covered by sea ice, surrounded by the tundra lands of Alaska, northern Canada, Greenland, northern Scandinavia and Siberia (Russia).
**Tundra** means the treeless area at high latitude (roughly above 60 degrees north) where it is too cold and the soil too frozen for trees to grow.
Cold environments are found at **high latitudes** (close to the poles) and at very high altitude in mountains.
**Polar regions** receive little solar energy since the sun is low in the sky; much sunlight that does arrive is reflected by white snow and ice (high albedo).
Cold environments have very **low biodiversity**, meaning few species, but the species present are specially adapted.
This point is about characteristics and adaptations; development and management of cold environments is in spec point 1.7.
core.h: What counts as a cold environment and where they are
core.p: **Cold environments** are places where temperatures are below freezing for much of the year and the growing season is very short. The spec focuses on **polar environments** (the Arctic and Antarctica, where permanent ice and snow cover the land) and **tundra environments** (treeless lands around the Arctic Ocean). They are found at high latitudes because the sun's rays strike the Earth at a low angle, so the energy is spread over a larger area and passes through more atmosphere, so there is little heating. Cold environments are some of the most fragile and least disturbed on Earth.

bullets: **Temperatures** stay below 0 degrees Celsius for most of the year; winters can reach minus 40 degrees Celsius or lower; the summers are short and cool.
**Annual temperature range** is large (the difference between the warmest and coldest month average).
**Precipitation** is low, usually under about 250 mm a year, mostly as snow, so the environments are technically a 'cold desert'.
Low temperatures mean low evaporation, so even small amounts of precipitation can leave the ground **wet in summer**.
**Daylight**: in summer the sun may stay above the horizon 24 hours a day ('midnight sun'), in winter there can be weeks or months of darkness (polar night).
**Strong winds** are common and increase the cold through wind chill, which makes it feel colder than the air temperature.
Antarctica is colder than the Arctic because it is a high continent covered with ice; the Arctic Ocean has a moderating effect.
core.h: Climate: very cold, dry and with extreme daylight
core.p: The climate of the polar and tundra regions has three defining features: **very low temperatures**, **low precipitation** and **extreme variation in daylight**. In the Arctic tundra winter temperatures are commonly well below minus 20 degrees Celsius, while the short summer is cool, with the warmest month averaging only a few degrees above freezing up to around 10 degrees. Precipitation is low, mostly falling as snow, so these areas are often called **cold deserts**. Because of the tilt of the Earth's axis there are periods of continuous daylight in summer and continuous darkness in winter.

bullets: Describe the **pattern**: 'temperatures are below 0 degrees Celsius for nine months of the year and only rise above 0 in June to August'.
Quote **values with units**, such as 'the coldest month is February at minus 27 degrees Celsius'.
**Temperature range** = highest monthly mean minus lowest monthly mean (for example 6 minus -27 = 33 degrees Celsius).
**Total precipitation** = add up the monthly bars; low totals show a cold desert.
Look for the **peak in precipitation**, which is often in late summer when the air is warmer and holds more moisture.
Note that precipitation falls mostly as snow in winter and as some rain in the short summer.
Link the data to the effects: short growing season (only 2-3 months above 0), frozen ground, and low plant growth.
core.p: Climate graphs are a favourite exam resource. Temperature is shown as a **line** against the left axis and precipitation as **bars** against the right axis. To describe the climate, give the overall pattern, then quote figures with units, then comment on seasonal change. You may need to calculate the **temperature range** (warmest minus coldest month) or the **total annual precipitation** (add all twelve bars). Always read the scales carefully because the two axes use different units.

bullets: The soils are **thin** (shallow) because weathering and soil formation are very slow in the cold.
Decomposition is very slow, so there is **little humus and few nutrients** (nutrients are locked up in dead material).
Soils are often **acidic** due to the peaty plant litter, which restricts what can grow.
The soil is frozen for most of the year, so **plant roots cannot penetrate deeply** and water cannot be absorbed.
Soil in the tundra is often **waterlogged in summer** because meltwater cannot drain through the frozen ground below.
Bare patches are slow to recover because new soil forms so slowly.
Link: poor soil means poor plant growth, which means little food for animals, showing interdependence.
core.h: Soils: thin, frozen, acidic and nutrient-poor
core.p: Tundra soils are **thin, poorly developed and low in nutrients**. The cold slows down the decomposition of dead plant material by bacteria and fungi, so little humus is added to the soil. Chemical weathering is also very slow. The soils are often **acidic**, and for most of the year they are **frozen**. Only in the summer does the top layer thaw, and even then the soil remains cold. This explains why only plants with low nutrient needs can grow here.

bullets: **Permafrost** = permanently frozen ground; the temperature of the ground stays below 0 degrees Celsius for years.
**Active layer** = the thin top layer of soil that thaws in summer and refreezes in winter.
Permafrost is **impermeable**, so surface water cannot soak away, producing waterlogged soil, bogs, ponds and marshes in summer.
The waterlogged, cold, acidic soil slows decomposition even more, so peat can build up.
Plants have **shallow roots** because they cannot grow into the permafrost.
Freeze-thaw (heaving) moves the soil and can tilt trees and buildings; engineers must build on stilts to avoid melting the permafrost.
If permafrost thaws, it can release stored carbon dioxide and methane, which speeds up climate change (a positive feedback).
core.p: **Permafrost** is ground (soil, rock and ice) that stays at or below 0 degrees Celsius for at least two consecutive years, and in the tundra it can be hundreds of metres deep. In summer the top layer of soil thaws; this is called the **active layer**. Because the permafrost below is frozen and **impermeable**, the meltwater cannot drain downwards, so the active layer becomes waterlogged, creating bogs, marshes and shallow lakes on flat land. The freeze and thaw cycle also moves and cracks the ground, forming patterned ground and uneven hummocks.

bullets: Plants: **mosses, lichens, sedges, grasses, wildflowers and dwarf shrubs**, which stay low to the ground.
**No trees** grow in the tundra because of cold, wind, frozen ground and short growing season (the tree line marks the southern edge).
The **growing season** is only about 50 to 90 days with temperatures high enough for growth.
**Low biodiversity** because few species can survive the extreme conditions.
Many plants are **perennials**, so they do not need to start from seed each year.
Vegetation is **slow-growing**, so trampling or vehicle tracks leave scars lasting decades.
In Antarctica there is almost no vegetation on land, only some mosses and lichens in ice-free areas; most life is in the surrounding sea.
core.p: There are **no trees** in the true tundra because the growing season is too short, the soil is frozen and shallow, and winds are strong. Vegetation consists of low plants that can survive in these conditions: **mosses, lichens, sedges, grasses, and dwarf shrubs** such as Arctic willow and bilberry, with bright flowers in the short summer. Plant growth is **slow**, so damage takes many years to recover. The plants are the **producers** at the base of the food web, supporting all other life.

bullets: **Low-growing, dwarf or cushion shape** gives shelter from the wind and reduces heat loss; some are covered by an insulating blanket of snow.
**Small, waxy or hairy leaves** reduce water loss and trap a layer of warm air, as in Arctic willow and Arctic poppy.
**Shallow roots** spread out in the thin active layer because the permafrost blocks deeper growth.
**Dark leaves/pigments** (such as red or purple) absorb more of the weak sunlight to warm the plant.
**Rapid life cycle**: plants flower and seed quickly in the 50 to 90 days of summer, then lie dormant over winter.
**Perennials** store food in roots or bulbs, so they can start growth quickly when the thaw arrives.
Some, like the **Arctic poppy**, have flowers that turn to follow the sun to concentrate heat on the centre of the flower.
core.p: Plants cope with the cold, wind, short summers and thin soil through **adaptations**, which are features that help an organism survive in its environment. Most tundra plants are **small and low growing** or cushion-shaped, which gives shelter from strong winds and keeps them in the warmer air near the ground, sometimes under snow cover. They have **shallow, spreading roots** that stay in the thawed active layer. They grow, flower and set seed **very quickly** during the brief summer. In each case, an exam answer must state the feature and explain how it helps survival.

bullets: **Arctic land animals**: caribou, musk ox, Arctic fox, Arctic hare, lemming, wolf, snowy owl; **marine**: polar bear (hunts seals on sea ice), seals, whales.
**Antarctic animals**: Emperor and Adelie penguins, seals, whales, and seabirds, which feed in the sea, not on the land.
Many **migrate** (for example caribou and birds such as the Arctic tern) to avoid the harsh winter and to reach food.
Some animals **hibernate** or shelter in dens or burrows to save energy and avoid the worst cold.
Animal populations are **small and sensitive**, because food is limited and breeding takes time.
Insect numbers are high in the summer on the waterlogged ground, providing food for migrating birds.
Biodiversity is low but each species plays a key role in the food web.
core.p: The tundra and polar regions support animals that are **well adapted** or move away in winter. On land, typical animals include Arctic foxes, Arctic hares, lemmings, musk oxen, caribou (reindeer), wolves, snowy owls and polar bears; marine life such as seals, whales, fish and krill is rich in the cold seas. In Antarctica, penguins, seals and seabirds depend on the sea for food. Many species are **migratory**, spending only the summer in the tundra when insects and plants are plentiful, while others stay all year and survive the winter by adaptations or hibernation.

bullets: **Thick fur and layers of fat (blubber)** trap heat and **insulate** the body, reducing heat loss in extremely cold conditions.
**White fur** provides **camouflage** against snow, helping predators like polar bears to hunt and prey like the Arctic hare and ptarmigan to hide.
**Small ears and short tails** (e.g. Arctic fox) reduce the surface area from which heat can be lost.
**Large, wide paws** spread the animal's weight over snow and thin ice, and have fur or rough pads for grip.
**Hibernation or denning** (polar bears, females den to give birth) conserves energy when food is short.
**Migration** takes animals to warmer areas or food-rich areas in winter (caribou, Arctic terns).
**Fat stores** built up in summer provide energy through the lean winter months.
core.h: Animal adaptations: polar bear and others
core.p: Animals adapt through **structural (body) features and behaviour**. The polar bear is the standard example. It has thick fur and a thick layer of fat (blubber) for insulation, a white coat for camouflage on snow and ice, small ears and a small body surface area for its size to reduce heat loss, and large furry paws that spread its weight on thin ice and provide grip. Other animals use similar features: the Arctic fox has a thick white winter coat, and the musk ox has long guard hair over a dense woolly undercoat. Always link the feature to the benefit.

bullets: **Producers** (mosses, lichens, grasses, and phytoplankton in the sea) make food using sunlight in the short summer.
**Primary consumers** (herbivores) such as lemmings, caribou and musk oxen eat the plants; **secondary consumers** such as the Arctic fox, owls and wolves eat them.
Marine food chain: **phytoplankton, krill, fish, seals, polar bear**; krill is the key food for many Antarctic animals.
**Climate controls soil** (permafrost and slow decomposition), **soil controls plants**, **plants control herbivores**, and herbivores control predators.
Food webs are **simple and short**, so they are easily upset by changes such as pollution, oil spills or warming.
**Decomposers** are very slow in the cold, so nutrients cycle slowly.
If a key species declines, the other species that depend on it also decline, showing **interdependence**.
core.p: In cold environments the climate, soil, water, plants and animals are all **interdependent**, which means that a change in one part affects the others. The cold climate creates permafrost, thin acidic soil and a short growing season, which limits the plants. Few plants mean limited food for herbivores, which limits predators. Food chains are short and simple, so the loss of one species can have a big effect. Examples: lichen is eaten by caribou, and caribou are eaten by wolves; in the sea, phytoplankton are eaten by krill, krill by fish and seals, and seals by polar bears.

bullets: **Fragile** = easily damaged by human activity or change and slow to recover.
Low temperatures slow **plant growth and decomposition**, so damage can last for many years.
Short, simple food chains mean **one change can affect many species**.
**Melting permafrost** damages roads and buildings and releases greenhouse gases.
**Melting sea ice** reduces hunting platforms for polar bears and seals and changes the ecosystem.
Cold environments are important as they store large amounts of **fresh water as ice** and carbon in frozen soil.
Link to 1.7: development (oil, gas, minerals, tourism and fishing) creates opportunities but needs careful management.
core.h: Why cold environments are fragile and why that matters
core.p: Cold environments are described as **fragile** because they are easily damaged and recover very slowly. Slow plant growth, thin soils, and the permafrost layer mean that disturbance such as vehicles, buildings, pipelines, or pollution can leave marks that last for decades. Climate change is warming the Arctic faster than most regions, causing permafrost to thaw and sea ice to shrink, which threatens habitats such as those of the polar bear. This is the basis for the case study and the management issues in the next spec point.

exam: 'Describe the climate' (2-3 marks): give the overall pattern plus data with units, such as 'temperatures are below 0 degrees Celsius for nine months, with a low of minus 27 degrees Celsius in February'.
For climate graph calculations show the working: temperature range = highest minus lowest; total precipitation = sum of the 12 monthly values; include units.
'Explain how a plant is adapted' (3-4 marks): feature + how it helps + link to the cold environment, for example 'small leaves reduce water loss, which helps in the dry, windy conditions'.
Polar bear adaptations are a stock question: thick fur, blubber (insulation), white coat (camouflage), small ears and large paws, each with its benefit.
For interdependence questions (up to 6 marks) write a chain: cold climate, then permafrost, then thin soil, then few plants, then few herbivores, then few predators.
Know the difference between 'describe' (what) and 'explain' (why); for soils and permafrost always add the reason, such as 'because the cold slows decomposition'.
Use accurate terms: permafrost, active layer, tundra, adaptation, biodiversity, interdependence; mark schemes reward correct terminology.
For food web questions name the producers, primary and secondary consumers, and explain that removing one species affects the others.
For 'why are cold environments fragile' give three linked reasons: slow plant growth, thin soils and permafrost, and short food chains.
Do not confuse Arctic and Antarctic: the Arctic is an ocean surrounded by land; Antarctica is a land mass covered in ice.

mistakes.r: It is cold because of its high latitude: the sun's rays are at a low angle, spread over a larger area and pass through more atmosphere, and snow reflects the sunlight.
mistakes.w: The tundra is cold because it is far from the sea.

mistakes.r: Precipitation is low (under about 250 mm), so it is a cold desert; snow only appears deep because it does not melt.
Roots are shallow because permafrost stops deeper growth, and the thin active layer is the only soil that thaws.
mistakes.w: Plants have shallow roots because they are lazy / the soil is dry.

mistakes.r: Waterlogging is due to meltwater that cannot drain through the impermeable permafrost, and low evaporation in the cold.
mistakes.w: The ground is waterlogged because of heavy rain.

mistakes.r: Fur and blubber trap heat and insulate the body, so less heat is lost to the cold air; describe the feature and how it helps.
mistakes.w: Animals have fur to keep them warm.

mistakes.r: The white fur provides camouflage, which helps them stalk seals without being seen.
mistakes.w: Polar bears are white to look nice / the bear is white because of snow.

mistakes.r: Biodiversity is low but plants such as mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs and animals such as caribou, Arctic fox and polar bear live there.
mistakes.w: There are no plants and animals in cold environments.

mistakes.r: Permafrost is permanently frozen ground (soil, rock and ice); snow is on the surface.

summary: The spec asks you to describe the characteristics of cold (polar and tundra) environments: their climate, soils, permafrost, vegetation and animals, how these are interdependent, and how plants and animals are adapted to the extreme conditions. It matters because cold environments are fragile and the adaptations and interdependence explain why they are easily damaged, which links to development and management.

terms.d: A cold, treeless environment at high latitudes with permafrost, low-growing plants and a very short growing season.
The very cold regions around the North and South Poles, covered by ice and snow for most of the year.
Ground that remains permanently frozen, at or below 0 degrees Celsius, for at least two years.
The top layer of soil in a permafrost area that thaws in summer and refreezes in winter.
A feature of an organism's body or behaviour that helps it to survive in its environment.
The variety of living things (plants and animals) in an area.
An environment that is easily damaged by change and takes a long time to recover.
The way living things and the physical parts of an environment (climate, soil, water) depend on and affect each other.
An organism, such as a plant or phytoplankton, that makes its own food by photosynthesis.
An organism that gets energy by eating other organisms.
A diagram of the many feeding links between organisms in an ecosystem.
Colouring or patterning that helps an animal blend into its surroundings so it cannot easily be seen.
A thick layer of fat under the skin of animals such as polar bears and seals that insulates them and stores energy.
The seasonal movement of animals from one area to another, often to find food or avoid harsh conditions.
The part of the year when temperatures and daylight are suitable for plant growth.
A state of very low activity in winter when an animal saves energy by lowering its body temperature and metabolism.

worked.ans: Polar bears have a thick layer of fat (blubber) and dense fur, which insulate the body and reduce heat loss in temperatures well below freezing (2). Their white coat gives camouflage on snow and ice, so they can approach seals without being seen (1). Their large, wide paws spread their weight on thin ice so they do not fall through (1). (4 marks)
worked.q: Explain how the polar bear is adapted to survive in a cold environment. (4 marks)
steps: For each: feature, then benefit in the cold environment.
Use terms like insulation, camouflage and surface area.

worked.ans: Temperature range = 6 - (-27) = 33 degrees Celsius (1). Total precipitation = 132 mm (1). The low total precipitation (under 250 mm) shows the area is a cold desert (1). The large temperature range shows long, very cold winters and a short, cool summer (1). (4 marks)
worked.q: A tundra climate graph shows a warmest month of 6 degrees Celsius and a coldest month of minus 27 degrees Celsius. Monthly precipitation is 5, 4, 4, 5, 5, 10, 25, 30, 20, 12, 7 and 5 mm. Calculate the temperature range and total annual precipitation, and say what these show. (4 marks)
steps: Comment: low total means a cold desert; large range shows strong seasonal contrast.

worked.ans: The tundra's very cold climate keeps the ground frozen as permafrost and slows decomposition, so the soil is thin, acidic and low in nutrients (2). In summer the meltwater cannot drain through the permafrost, so the active layer is waterlogged. Only small plants such as mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs with shallow roots can survive, and they grow slowly in the short growing season (2). These plants feed herbivores like caribou and lemmings, which are eaten by predators such as the Arctic fox and wolf. Because food chains are short and simple, a change in one part, such as a cold summer reducing plant growth, reduces the food for animals higher up and affects the whole ecosystem, showing interdependence (2). (6 marks)
worked.q: Explain how the climate, soil, plants and animals of the tundra are interdependent. (6 marks)
steps: Start with climate: very cold, low precipitation, short summer.
Link to permafrost and thin, acidic, nutrient-poor soils.
Link to low-growing plants, then herbivores and predators, with a named food chain and a consequence of a change.
